title: A pricing page for a B2B SaaS company
metaTitle: A B2B SaaS pricing page that shows fit
excerpt: Operators use a B2B pricing page to judge fit. Show what is included, what is not, and how to book a demo. Do not hide the shape of the price.
alt: A bright office window ledge with a laptop, a closed notebook, white chairs, and a tall indoor tree. The article is about judging a pricing page in a calm, practical read.
caption: Pricing is read in ordinary daylight, next to a notebook the buyer may not even open. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs on a B2B SaaS pricing page?
faqs.answer: Show the unit of the price, what each plan includes, and what it leaves out. Name how to book a demo for the part a table cannot settle. The page is a fit test for someone who can already do the arithmetic.

faqs.question: Should a SaaS company hide its price?
faqs.answer: Publish the shape if buyers will ask for it anyway. A seat price, a usage unit, or a clear statement that a plan is custom above a named threshold is enough. Hiding a number you already know spends the demo on a fact the page could have carried.

faqs.question: How should a demo relate to pricing?
faqs.answer: The demo is for fit a table cannot show, such as their workflow or a security question. It should not be a toll for seeing a public number. If a plan can be bought without a call, give that plan a straight path.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A B2B SaaS company pricing page is where an operator who already runs software judges fit. They are not there to do arithmetic. They want to see what is included, what is not, and how to book a demo if the shape matches the way they buy.

Hide the shape and they will ask anyway, on a call you could have skipped or in a tab you will never see. A page that says "contact us for pricing" when the offer is a published seat price wastes the visit. A page that publishes a number and hides the limits wastes the call. Show the shape. Then offer the demo for the part a table cannot settle.

## Fit comes before the total

An operator arrives with a rough budget and a rough headcount. They can multiply. What they cannot invent is the boundary. Is the price per seat, per workspace, or per record? Does the demo account count? Is support inside the number or a line that appears later?

Put that shape in the first screen. Name the unit. Name who the plan is for. If there are three plans, say which one a team of their kind usually starts on, and why. The recommendation is a form of honesty. A wall of equal columns forces them to become the analyst.

Nielsen Norman Group's account of page visits is useful here. People often have time to read only about a quarter of the words on a page they do open. A pricing page that explains philosophy for six paragraphs and parks the unit at the bottom will be skimmed past the point. The unit, the inclusion, and the exclusion have to sit where a skim still catches them.

Write the numbers you are willing to say in public. If a plan is custom, say custom, and say what makes it custom. Volume, security review, a deployment you host for them. "Custom" as a way to avoid a conversation is a closed door. "Custom above a named threshold" is a shape.

## What is included

Each plan needs a short list of what the buyer actually receives. Use their words. Seats. Records. Environments. The admin role. The audit log. Email support. A named success manager, if that is true.

Tie each line to a job when the line would otherwise be vague. "SSO" is clearer as "people sign in with the company account." "API access" is clearer as "your team can read and write records without the interface." You can keep the short name. Add the job in the same line.

Keep the list comparable across plans. If the middle plan adds the audit log, the cheaper plan should show the audit log as absent, not merely omit it. Omission reads as a trick once the buyer notices. A quiet "not included" is kinder than a surprise in procurement.

Say what happens at the edge. Extra seats. Extra records. A month when they go over. The operator is imagining the bad month, not the brochure month. A sentence on overage, or a sentence that there is no overage and the plan simply stops, belongs next to the price.

## What is not included

The exclusions are the fit test. Implementation that you do not do. Data migration beyond a file upload. A legal review of their industry. On-premise hosting. Training for a team of two hundred. If the product is the software and the rest is their work, say so beside the plan, not in a footnote after the contract.

This is also where a services offer either belongs or does not. If you sell onboarding as a paid block, name the block and the boundary. How many workshops. What you will not configure. The next step for that block can be the same demo, with a note that the call will separate software from services. A blended page that mixes a seat price with an unnamed project fee makes the operator guess which number is real.

Google's guidance on people-first content asks you to answer the question the visitor brought, from knowledge you actually have. On this page the question is "what would we be buying?" A list of adjectives does not answer it. Included and excluded do.

Leave a line for the thing you are often asked and do not sell. "We do not replace your accountant." "We do not send the campaign for you." The sentence costs little and prevents a demo spent on the wrong hope.

## How the demo sits next to the price

The demo is for fit that a table cannot show. Their data model. Their approval chain. A security question. It is not a toll you charge for the right to see a number you already know.

Put "Book a demo" on the plan that needs a conversation, and also as a quiet path for the person who understands the price and still wants to see the product. If a plan can be bought without a call, give it a straight purchase path and do not force the demo. Forcing a meeting onto a self-serve plan tells the operator you do not trust your own page.

Say what to have ready. A sense of seat count. The system this would replace or sit beside. The name of the person who has to approve. That preparation makes the call shorter and makes the page feel like a brief, not a funnel.

If you are not ready to name a price, you can still show the shape. Per seat, annual, minimum of ten, implementation quoted from a menu. Then the demo has something to confirm. A blank page plus a button asks them to book in order to learn whether they were the audience. Many will not.

## Plans that hide the shape

A few patterns keep showing up on pages that feel finished and still fail the operator.

The toggle between monthly and annual changes the number and hides the fact that annual is the only plan you will actually sell. Show both if both are real. If annual is the offer, say that monthly is a trial length, not a lifestyle.

The enterprise column is a list of every feature with a "talk to us" button and no hint of the unit. Add one sentence. Priced on records, or on a security review plus seats. The buyer can then decide if the call is worth the hour.

The cheapest plan is a demo of the expensive plan, with the job-doing features removed. If the cheap plan cannot do the job the homepage promised, do not let it be the first column. Lead with the plan that matches the job. Put the limited plan where it reads as a limit.

A calculator that asks for twelve inputs before it shows a range is arithmetic dressed as product. Offer it after the shape is visible, for the person who wants to model a year. The first screen is the shape, not the spreadsheet.

## Write the page so a skim can decide

Use a structure a tired operator can parse.

1. One sentence on who the pricing is for.
2. The unit and the plan you recommend for that buyer.
3. Included, in their words.
4. Not included, in the same view.
5. A note on overage, term, and what changes at renewal if you know it.
6. Book a demo, with what the call is for and what to bring.

Keep the type large enough to read on a phone. Pricing pages die when the comparison becomes a horizontal scroll of tiny text. Stack the recommended plan first on a narrow screen. Let the others follow. A desktop table can exist. It should not be the only way to learn the shape.

Read the lines aloud. If a line only makes sense to the person who built the billing system, rewrite it. "Workspace" might mean a company to you and a project to them. Pick the word they already use and define it once.

When the price shape is clear, the next question is what work you actually do around the software. A services block written as vague capabilities will undo the clarity you just earned. Read [how to write the services page in the buyer's language](/blog/the-services-page-a-b2b-saas-company-actually-needs) before you add a row of abstract nouns under the plans.

If you want to see how a studio handles the same kind of clarity on its own site, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The standard is the same. Show the thing, show the boundary, and let the next step be obvious.

## Before you publish the numbers

Check the page against the contract, not against the slide. If the order form includes a platform fee the page never names, fix the page. The operator who feels tricked will not argue about your typeface.

Check that the demo label matches the calendar. If the button says demo and the form asks for a novel about their stack, you have built a contact page and called it pricing. Move the long form off this path or cut it down to what the call requires.

Check the title of the page. It should say pricing, and it should be specific enough that a shared link makes sense in a procurement thread. A clever title that hides the word forces the buyer to explain your joke to their finance lead.

Then stop. A pricing page does not need a brand film. It needs a shape an operator can accept or refuse before they book the hour.
